implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library has the pieces but not the pattern: Mutex plus Thread::ConditionVariable (or Thread::Queue) can be composed into a latch or a phase barrier by hand, and Thread#join covers the plain fan-in. The dominant realization is the concurrent-ruby gem, which ships the objects directly: Concurrent::CountDownLatch#count_down with #wait(timeout) is the one-shot gate - the documentation states it can be used only once and its value cannot be reset - while Concurrent::CyclicBarrier provides the reusable rendezvous. Keep the stdlib composition for small scripts with no gem dependency, and remember that MRI threads parallelize I/O but not CPU work.
code_sketch:
require "concurrent"
done = Concurrent::CountDownLatch.new(workers.size)      # one-shot: cannot be reset
workers.each do |w|
  Thread.new do
    w.call
  ensure
    done.count_down                                       # every exit path
  end
end
abort "timed out" unless done.wait(30)                   # false on timeout, not an exception
phase = Concurrent::CyclicBarrier.new(n)                 # reusable rendezvous
pitfalls: Thread::ConditionVariable#wait must be called while holding the associated mutex and wrapped in a predicate loop; a bare wait wakes on spurious signals and can miss the release entirely.

The stdlib composition is easy to get wrong on the failure path: an exception in a thread body without an ensure block skips count_down and the waiter blocks until its timeout, so signal completion from ensure.
CountDownLatch#wait returns false on timeout instead of raising - ignoring the boolean turns a timeout into a silent early continuation.
MRI's GVL keeps CPU-bound phases effectively serial, and Ractors cannot share the mutable synchronization object at all, so cross-process or cross-Ractor coordination needs a different mechanism.
